# Opening case: Christ had no biological father

**Position.** Christ had no human biological father. The KJV says Mary was a virgin and that "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20). It never names a man as the source of the conception.

---

## 1. Mary was a virgin when the child was conceived

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L2]** The word is *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin." Luke uses it twice in this one verse, and Matthew 1:23 uses it again.

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097) means "to know," and here it means marital knowledge. *Anēr* (G435) means "a man, a husband." Mary's "I know not a man" is her stated reason why a conception seems impossible. The angel does not answer by naming a man.

**[L3]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" is *ʿalmāh* (H5959), "a virgin of marriageable age." Genesis 24:43 uses the same word of Rebekah: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." Genesis 24:16 shows what the word covers: "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23 quotes the prophecy and applies it: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L4]** From Luke 1:27 and 1:34 [L1], the Greek *parthenos* and *ginōskō* [L2], and Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23 [L3], I infer that the conception was announced to a woman who had known no man. A man's seed is therefore not the stated cause of the conception.

---

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, not a man

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Sunerchomai* (G4905) means "to come together," and here it refers to the marriage union. *Ek* (G1537) means "out of, from the source of," so "of the Holy Ghost" gives the origin. *Pneuma hagion* (G4151, G40) means "holy spirit."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Conceived" translates *gennēthen* (from *gennaō*, G1080), "begotten, brought forth." The source is again *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537, G4151, G40), "out of the Holy Spirit."

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Eperchomai* (G1904) means "to come upon." *Episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow." *Dio kai* means "therefore also," and it makes the Holy Ghost's coming the reason for the title "Son of God."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1] both use *ek* (G1537) for the source [L2]. Luke 1:35 names the agents as the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and says the child is "born of thee" [L3]. I infer that the text assigns the generating cause to the Holy Ghost and the bodily source to Mary alone. No male human is given a part.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," in a clause that names the woman's seed and not a man's: "between thy seed and her seed." **[L2]** The Hebrew is *zeraʿ* (H2233), "seed." **[L4]** On those two footings, a line that is traced through the woman fits the text's pattern here.

---

## 3. Matthew's genealogy stops saying "begat" at Joseph, and Joseph is shown not to be the father

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every earlier link uses *gennaō* (G1080) in the active, "begat." In 1:16 the verb becomes passive, *egennēthē*, "was born." The relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular, so it points to Mary alone and not to Joseph.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097) is the same word as in Luke 1:34, and it is negated here. *Heōs hou* means "until which time." Joseph is described as "her husband" but as one who "knew her not" before the birth.

**[L4]** Joseph "was minded to put her away" (Matthew 1:19) [L1] because Mary "was found with child" "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18) [L3]. A husband who knew himself to be the father would have had no cause to put her away. The *gennaō* (G1080) pattern also breaks at 1:16 [L2]. I infer that the text excludes Joseph as the begetter and still calls him "husband."

---

## 4. Texts that call Joseph the father report supposition or speech, and the text corrects them

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Nomizō* (G3543) means "to hold by custom or opinion." The word marks a belief held, not a fact stated.

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**[L3]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L4]** In Luke 2:48 [L1] the speaker says "thy father" of Joseph, who was Mary's husband. In Luke 2:49 [L3] the child answers by pointing to "my Father's business." That the child does so right after "thy father" shows a different Father is in view. Luke 3:23 [L1] marks the common opinion with *nomizō* (G3543) [L2], so I infer these verses do not assert that Joseph begat him.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20 calls Joseph "thou son of David." **[L4]** This names Joseph's own lineage and the legal standing he had as Mary's husband (Matthew 1:16, "the husband of Mary" [L3]). It does not say that Joseph's seed was in the child.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Mary was a virgin who knew no man when the conception was announced. Footing: Luke 1:27 and 1:34 [L1] with *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") and *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") [L2], and Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23 [L3].
2. The text assigns the conception to the Holy Ghost, not to a man. Footing: Matthew 1:20 [L1] with *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537, G4151, G40, "out of the Holy Spirit") [L2], and Luke 1:35 with Matthew 1:18 [L3].
3. Matthew 1:16 changes from "begat" to "of whom was born," and Joseph is shown not to be the begetter. Footing: Matthew 1:16 [L1] with *gennaō* (G1080, "to beget") passive and *hēs* (feminine "of whom") [L2], and Matthew 1:19 with 1:25 [L3].
4. Texts naming Joseph as father report supposition or speech and are corrected. Footing: Luke 3:23 [L1] with *nomizō* (G3543, "to suppose by opinion") [L2], and Luke 2:48 with 2:49 [L3].
5. Christ had no biological father among men. He was conceived of the Holy Ghost in Mary, a virgin. Footing: links 1 to 4 above, resting on Matthew 1:20 [L1], *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537, G4151, G40) [L2], and Luke 1:35 [L3].

# Defender, Round 2

I grant three points before answering. Each is a discipline, not a loss.

- **Genesis 24:16.** The word there is *bᵉthûlâh* (H1330, "virgin"), not *ʿalmâh* (H5959). I withdraw that verse as lexical footing for H5959.
- **Genesis 3:15.** Genesis 4:25 ("hath appointed me another seed") shows "her seed" can belong to a child with a father. I withdraw Genesis 3:15 as independent proof.
- **"Corrected" in D4.** The challenger says "both stand." I narrow D4 to this: Luke 2:48 is speech and Luke 3:23 is a marked supposition. Neither asserts a begetting.

---

## 1. Answer to UNSUPPORTED-L4 1 and 2 (D1: timing, and the word *ʿalmâh*)

**On the word.**
- **[L1]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw [water]."
- **[L2]** *ʿalmâh* (H5959) stands in this verse, and the KJV renders it "virgin."
- **[L3]** Genesis 24:16 describes the same Rebekah as "a virgin, neither had any man known her."
- **[L4]** The KJV uses "virgin" for H5959 in Genesis 24:43 of a woman the next verse-set describes as one no man had known. It does the same in Isaiah 7:14 [L1, L2]. The weight of D1 does not rest on the Hebrew. It rests on Matthew 1:23, where the KJV gives "a virgin" for *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin"), and on Luke 1:27, where *parthenos* is said of Mary twice.

**On the time.** I grant that Luke 1:31 puts the conception after the announcement and that Luke 1:34 is present tense. The rows then close the interval.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:39: "And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:42: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:43: "that the mother of my Lord should come to me?"
- **[L1]** Luke 1:56: "And Mary abode with her about three months, and returned to her own house."
- **[L2]** *Gastēr* (G1064, "womb") stands behind Luke 1:31, where the conception is "in thy womb."
- **[L4]** Mary goes "with haste" and is called "the mother of my Lord," with "fruit" in her womb, on arrival (Luke 1:39, 1:42-43). She then returns "to her own house" (Luke 1:56). Matthew 1:18 says that "before they came together, she was found with child." The conception falls within the haste of Luke 1:39. No coming together lies between announcement and conception.

## 2. Answer to the press on "of the Holy Ghost," *dio kai*, and 1 John 5:1 (D2, C3)

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"

- **[L2]** *Gennaō* (G1080) is, in the lexicon, "properly, of the father." The KJV margin renders it "begotten." In this verse *ek* (G1537, "out of") sets the Holy Ghost as the source of what is begotten "in her."
- **[L1]** The verse opens with "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for…". The ground (*gar*) given for the command is the Holy Ghost's origin.
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:18-19 give Joseph's cause for fear: she "was found with child" and he "was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L4]** The angel meets Joseph's fear about the pregnancy by naming its origin (Matthew 1:20), not by naming Joseph. This rests on Matthew 1:20 [L1] and its *ek* with *gennaō* [L2], and on Matthew 1:18-19 [L3].

**On 1 John 5:1.**
- **[L3]** John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **[L2]** *Gennaō* (G1080) is "figuratively, to regenerate," as the lexicon gives it.
- **[L4]** 1 John 5:1 [L1] says "born of God" of believers. John 1:13 [L3] sets that "of God" over against "the will of man." So the 1 John parallel is a source-claim opposed to human will. It does not set a human begetter beside God. Matthew 1:20 has the thing "conceived in her," in her womb, "of the Holy Ghost."

**On Luke 1:35.**
- **[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") stands in the same verse, directly after the clause naming the Holy Ghost's coming and the power's overshadowing. That clause is its stated antecedent.
- **[L3]** Luke 1:34 asks "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?", and Luke 1:35 begins "And the angel answered." The answer to the how-question is the Holy Ghost's coming.
- **[L4]** The "therefore" gives the Holy Ghost's coming as the stated reason for "the Son of God." This rests on Luke 1:35 [L1] and the position of *dio kai* [L2], and on Luke 1:34 as the question being answered [L3].

**On 1 Chronicles 28:6 and 2 Samuel 7:14.**
- **[L1]** 1 Chronicles 28:6: "for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
- **[L3]** 2 Samuel 7:12 states of Solomon that the seed "shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- **[L4]** For Solomon, God's fatherhood is a choosing ("[to be]" is the KJV's italic), and David's bowels are named in the same promise (1 Chronicles 28:6, 2 Samuel 7:12). For Christ, the conception rows state the Holy Ghost as source (Matthew 1:20) and the womb as place (Luke 1:31). The two cases differ in what the rows say.

## 3. Answer to the press on Matthew 1:16 and 1:19 (D3)

**Matthew 1:3, 1:5, 1:16.**
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." Matthew 1:5: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth."
- **[L2]** *Gennaō* (G1080) is active ("begat") in each clause, with the man as subject, and the mother is marked with *ek* ("of").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
- **[L2]** In the second clause of 1:16 *gennaō* is passive, "was born," and the relative is feminine singular, *ex hēs*. Joseph appears as *anēr* (G435, "husband"), the relation to Mary, not as the subject of "begat."
- **[L4]** In 1:3 and 1:5 the man and the mother stand in one clause, with "begat" governing both (Matthew 1:3, 1:5). In 1:16 "begat" ends at Joseph, and the next clause has only the mother's relative and the passive verb (Matthew 1:16). I grant that *ek* marks mothers in all three. What differs is that the man's "begat" is absent from the final clause.

**Matthew 1:19.** The press says Joseph's purpose is only about exposure. The meaning I assign is that a husband who knew himself the father would have no cause to put her away.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child." The cause of the intent is the finding of a pregnancy where no coming together had occurred.
- **[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife." So "her husband" and "thy wife" in Matthew 1:19-20 are the text's usage for the espoused, and carry no sign of knowing.
- **[L4]** The two grounds in Matthew 1:19 ("just" and "not willing to make her a publick example") both presuppose a charge worth exposing. The charge is the pregnancy "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18). The angel's answer then addresses the pregnancy's origin (Matthew 1:20). A pregnancy Joseph knew to be his own gives no ground for a "put away" at all. This rests on Matthew 1:18-19 [L1/L3] and on *kai* joining the two participles in one purpose [L2].

## 4. Answer to C4 (the keystone): "Joseph knew Mary within the espousal"

- **[L1]** Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." The order is knowing, then conceiving.
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- **[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") is negated by *ou* in Matthew 1:25 and stands in Luke 1:34. *Heōs hou* means "until which time."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child." Luke 2:5: "To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child."
- **[L4]** The dilemma has two horns.
  - If Joseph knew her before the finding, that is a coming together before "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18).
  - If he knew her after the taking (Matthew 1:24), it is after the pregnancy already found (Matthew 1:18), and "knew her not till she had brought forth" (Matthew 1:25) denies it through the birth.
  - Luke 2:5 still calls her "espoused" when "great with child," after the taking.

  Genesis 4:1's order, knowing and then conceiving, finds no place in Matthew 1:18-25. The challenger's "within the espousal" has no row.

## 5. Answer to C1/C2 and the question on Hebrews 7:14

**Question: how is it "evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda," given Numbers 1:2, 18?**
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
- **[L2]** *Prodēlos* (G4271) means "plain before all, evident." It speaks of what is manifest in the record.
- **[L3]** Luke 2:4-5: Joseph went to be taxed "because he was of the house and lineage of David," "with Mary his espoused wife." Matthew 1:21 and 1:25: "thou shalt call his name JESUS" / "and he called his name JESUS."
- **[L3]** Deuteronomy 25:6: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel."
- **[L4]** Numbers 1:18 sets the pedigree record "by the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:2, 1:18). Deuteronomy 25:6 shows the same canon carrying a name and house in Israel to a son the man did not beget. Joseph, "of the house and lineage of David," registered with Mary and named the child (Luke 2:4-5, Matthew 1:25). So the tribe is evident by the record of the house, and the record does not require a begetting. Luke 3:23 itself marks Joseph's sonship of the child as "supposed" [L1/L2, *enomizeto*, G3543].

**Acts 2:30, Romans 1:3, Hebrews 7:10.**
- **[L1]** Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."
- **[L3]** Acts 2:30 names "the fruit of his loins" of David. Luke 1:32 gives "the throne of his father David" to the child Mary shall conceive (Luke 1:31).
- **[L2]** *Osphys* (G3751, "loins") is said in Hebrews 7:10 of Levi in the loins of Abraham, who was his great-grandfather. That is the idiom of descent across generations.
- **[L4]** "Loins" language names the forefather, not a particular intermediate man (Hebrews 7:10, Acts 2:30). C1's step to "Joseph's loins" is not in Acts 2:30, which names David's.

**Mary's line.**
- **[L1]** Luke 3:23: "which was [the son] of Heli."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph."
- **[L4]** Two records give Joseph's father as Jacob (Matthew 1:16) and "of Heli" (Luke 3:23, where "[the son]" is the KJV's italic). This fits a second line, but I rest the case on Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:35, not on this.

**On Luke 2:48-50.**
- **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee."
- **[L3]** Luke 2:49: "my Father's business." Luke 2:50: "they understood not the saying which he spake unto them." Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled."
- **[L4]** "Thy father" is Mary's speech. The narrator himself writes "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33). The child's reply says "my Father's business," and Luke 2:50 records that they did not take it in. This shows "my Father" was not already received as common knowledge. It does not assert a begetting by Joseph.

---
